::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_oksoda()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_oksoda()`, built from OK Soda cans (1993 to 1995): a brushed silver background, a black frame, a gray comic panel, OK red marks and title, slate and brick accents, and a Courier New title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1014)
ok_soda_sales <- tibble(
  store_id = 1:300,
  cans = round(rnorm(n = 300, mean = 45, sd = 12))
)
labs_histogram <- labs(
  title = "OK Soda",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Cans sold per store in one day",
  x = "Cans sold")
ggp2_hist <- ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
     aes(x = cans)) + 
     geom_histogram() 
ggp2_hist + 
  labs_histogram
```

::::

## Description 

A histogram is a graph that displays numerical data spread over a time frame or interval. Each bar shows the frequency of data points within a specific range. Unlike bar graphs, histograms do not have gaps between the bars, indicating that data covers a continuous interval. The x-axis displays the variable range, while the y-axis represents observation frequency.

Unlike a typical bar graph, histograms can be used to visually assess the '[normality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution)' (i.e. *are the bars symmetrical, with a single peak in the middle of the `x` axis?* Or *do the bars form multiple peaks?*) or '[skewness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness)' (i.e., *is there a long 'tail' of bars with decreasing length on either end of the `x` axis?*) of a variable's distribution.

In `ggplot2`, histograms can be built using [`geom_histogram()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html).

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

Install packages.


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

OK Soda was Coca-Cola's 1993 soda for Gen X, sold in gray comic book cans with slogans like "Things are going to be OK." We'll simulate one day of sales at 300 test market stores with `rnorm()`, rounding each store's sales to a whole number of cans. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 values every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1014)
ok_soda_sales <- tibble(
  store_id = 1:300,
  cans = round(rnorm(n = 300, mean = 45, sd = 12))
)
glimpse(ok_soda_sales)
```
:::

## Distribution

You don't have to be a statistician to read a histogram, but it helps to know what shape you should expect. Because we generated `cans` ourselves, we already know the answer: every value came from a [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) with a mean of 45 cans and a standard deviation of 12 cans. Below we'll move from the numbers, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten stores.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: concrete_values_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(ok_soda_sales$cans, 10)
```
:::

Most of these values land within 12 cans of 45, and a few (like 16 and 23) sit further out. If we sort all 300 stores into three ranges (below one standard deviation, within one standard deviation, and above one standard deviation), the middle range holds most of the stores.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: concrete_counts_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
ok_soda_ranges <- ok_soda_sales |>
  mutate(range = cut(cans,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 33, 57, Inf),
    labels = c("under 33", "33 to 56", "57 and over"),
    right = FALSE)) |>
  count(range)
ok_soda_ranges
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model shows these counts as parts of one whole. The full bar is all 300 stores, and the middle part takes up roughly two thirds of it.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pictorial_bar_model_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
ggplot(data = ok_soda_ranges,
    aes(x = n, y = "300 stores", fill = range)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE),
    color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white",
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Number of stores", y = NULL,
    fill = "Cans sold")
```
:::

A histogram is the same idea, cut into 30 thinner pieces and stood upright. The dashed lines below mark 33 and 57 cans, the edges of the middle part of the bar model.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pictorial_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
    aes(x = cans)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(33, 57), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Cans sold")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The `rnorm()` call that created the data is a single statement:

$$
X \sim \text{Normal}(\mu = 45, \sigma = 12)
$$

The mean ($\mu$) sets where the tallest bars sit on the `x` axis, and the standard deviation ($\sigma$) sets how far the bars spread out from it. For a normal distribution, roughly 68% of values fall within one $\sigma$ of $\mu$ and 95% fall within two. Our simulated stores come close: `r round(mean(ok_soda_sales$cans >= 33 & ok_soda_sales$cans < 57) * 100)`% are within one $\sigma$ and `r round(mean(ok_soda_sales$cans >= 21 & ok_soda_sales$cans < 69) * 100)`% are within two.

The small gap between the rule and our sample is just sampling variation. Change the number in `set.seed()` and the bars shift, but the bell shape stays centered near 45 cans.


## Grammar 

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::



1. Create labels with `labs()`

2. Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

3. Assign `cans` to the `x`

4. Add the `geom_histogram()`

5. Adjust the `bins` accordingly 

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_histogram
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_histogram <- labs(
  title = "OK Soda",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Cans sold per store in one day",
  x = "Cans sold")

ggp2_hist <- ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
     aes(x = cans)) + 
     geom_histogram() 

ggp2_hist + 
  labs_histogram
```
:::


::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_histogram
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_histogram <- labs(
  title = "OK Soda",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Cans sold per store in one day",
  x = "Cans sold")

ggp2_hist <- ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
     aes(x = cans)) + 
     geom_histogram() 

ggp2_hist + 
  labs_histogram
```



The standard number of bins is `30`, but ['you should always override this value, exploring multiple widths to find the best to illustrate the stories in your data.'](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html)


```{r}
#| label: bins_histogram
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: show
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
ggp2_hist_bins45 <- ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
     aes(x = cans)) + 
     geom_histogram(bins = 45) 

ggp2_hist_bins45 + 
  labs_histogram

ggp2_hist_bins15 <- ggplot(data = ok_soda_sales,
     aes(x = cans)) + 
     geom_histogram(bins = 15) 

ggp2_hist_bins15 + 
  labs_histogram
```
